bull.argument: The filing shows a company compounding its core business. Net sales rose 10% to $297,247 million, comparable sales grew 8% (7% excluding currency and gasoline), and digitally-enabled comparable sales jumped 21%. Net income increased 14% to $9,226 million, or $20.76 per diluted share. Membership fee revenue grew 11%, and the U.S. and Canada renewal rate held at 92.3%, a sign of member loyalty that underpins the model. Operating cash flow rose to $15,817 million from $13,335 million, funding $6,435 million of capex with cash left over, and the board raised the quarterly dividend 13%. The company plans up to 33 new warehouses in 2027 and about $7,500 million of capex. Management also reports that the gross margin in core merchandise rose 15 basis points as a percentage of its own sales, a sign of pricing discipline. The risks are real: heavy reliance on California and Canada, tariffs, and AI-driven competition. Still, the filing shows the economics working, with growing cash generation, a rising dividend, and a loyal membership base.

claims.claim: Core earnings and cash generation grew strongly in 2026.
claims.quote: Net income increased 14% to $9,226, $20.76 per diluted share, compared to $8,099, $18.21 per diluted share in 2025

claims.claim: Member loyalty remains high, supporting recurring fee revenue.
claims.quote: At the end of 2026, member renewal rates were 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada and 89.8% worldwide.

claims.claim: Operating cash flow grew and funds expansion and shareholder returns.
claims.quote: Net cash provided by operating activities totaled $15,817 in 2026, compared to $13,335 in 2025.

bear.argument: The bear case rests on concentration and fragility. The filing says U.S. and Canadian operations produced 86% and 83% of net sales and operating income, and California alone is 26% of U.S. net sales, a dependence the company itself calls high. Growth is increasingly fragile: the company says sites are harder to secure, new warehouses carry lower initial profitability and can cannibalize existing ones, and the plan calls for up to 33 openings and roughly $7,500 million of capex in 2027, up from $6,435 million. Margins are thin, with gross margin at 11.09%, down three basis points, and the filing warns that modest changes in merchandise costs or SG&A can have substantial impacts on net income. The 10% sales growth was flattered by $3,501 million from higher gasoline prices, and the IEEPA tariff refunds of $184 million are one-time items the company says it is investing back into member prices. The filing also says the stock price reflects high market expectations, so any shortfall could push it lower.

claims.claim: Earnings depend heavily on a concentrated base of U.S. and Canadian operations and on California.
claims.quote: Within the U.S., we are highly dependent on our California operations, which comprised 26% of U.S. net sales in 2026.

claims.claim: Growth through new warehouses carries lower initial profitability and cannibalization risk.
claims.quote: Negative aspects of such growth include lower initial operating profitability relative to existing warehouses and cannibalization of sales at existing warehouses when openings occur in existing markets.

claims.claim: Sales growth was boosted by gasoline prices, and the stock price already reflects high expectations.
claims.quote: We believe that the price of our stock currently reflects high market expectations for our future operating results.

bull.argument: The bear case is right that concentration and thin margins are real, but the filing shows they are being managed, not ignored. Yes, U.S. and Canadian operations generated 86% and 83% of net sales and operating income, yet the company discloses that dependence openly and lists the specific risks. The gasoline point is fair, but it cuts both ways: the filing says gasoline added 130 basis points to net sales growth, while excluding gasoline price inflation, gross margin rose 10 basis points to 11.22%. Core comparable sales grew 7% excluding currency and gasoline, a cleaner signal of demand. Digitally-enabled comparable sales rose 21%. On tariffs, the $184 million of refunds is a real cash benefit, and the $155 million received afterward shows the stream continues, even if management plans to reinvest most of it in member value. On growth, the 33 planned openings and $7,500 million of capex are funded by $15,817 million of operating cash flow and $21,301 million of cash and short-term investments. Members renewed at 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada. The high expectations point is a fair risk, but it is a reason to watch execution, not evidence of weakness.

claims.claim: Core sales growth held up after stripping out gasoline and currency effects.
claims.quote: Increases in comparable sales excluding the impact of changes in foreign-currency and gasoline prices (1) : U.S. 7 % 7 % 5 %

claims.claim: Growth investment is funded from internal cash and liquidity.
claims.quote: We believe that our cash and investment positions and operating cash flow, with capacity under existing and available credit agreements, will be sufficient to meet our liquidity and capital requirements for the foreseeable future

claims.claim: Member loyalty remains strong despite the bear's concerns about growth quality.
claims.quote: At the end of 2026, member renewal rates were 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada and 89.8% worldwide.

bear.argument: The opponent's cash story leans on figures that the filing qualifies. Of the $21,301 million in cash and short-term investments, $2,842 million is unsettled card receivables, which the filing says generally settle within four days. Operating cash flow of $15,817 million rose partly because of 'reduced net investment in merchandise inventories,' driven by faster inventory turns and improved supplier payment terms. That is a working-capital tailwind that may not repeat. The 11.22% gross margin is a non-GAAP figure that excludes gasoline inflation. Reported gross margin fell to 11.09%, and the filing says the core-category margin decline of 11 basis points was offset by mix. The 130-basis-point gasoline boost to sales is also a reported effect, so headline growth depends partly on fuel prices the company does not control. Concentration is also a risk, not just a disclosure: 86% of net sales and 83% of operating income come from U.S. and Canadian operations, and the filing says thin margins mean 'modest changes' in merchandise costs or SG&A can have 'substantial impacts on net income.' The filing's own warning that expectations are already high makes that sensitivity matter.

claims.claim: Cash on hand overstates free liquidity, because part of it is card receivables that settle within days.
claims.quote: Of these balances, unsettled credit and debit card receivables represented $2,842 and $2,670.

claims.claim: Operating cash flow was helped by a working-capital benefit from inventory and supplier terms.
claims.quote: The latter was a result of faster inventory turns and improved payment terms with suppliers.

claims.claim: Thin margins make earnings highly sensitive to small cost changes, and the stock already prices in high expectations.
claims.quote: Because our business operates on very low margins, modest changes in various items in the consolidated statements of income, particularly merchandise costs and SG&A expenses, can have substantial impacts on net income.

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes, but the bear's quotes more directly support its points about cash quality, working-capital tailwinds, and margin sensitivity, and it rebutted the bull's cash and non-GAAP margin claims with specific filing language. The bull's rebuttal leaned on the 11.22% ex-gasoline margin and reused a renewal-rate quote from Round 1 without addressing the bear's sensitivity and cash-quality arguments as directly.
